overview: The Raspberry Pi 5 is the same 'real Linux computer' idea as the Pi 4 — it boots an OS from a microSD card, multitasks, and runs regular Python/C++ programs instead of firmware — but the underlying architecture changed enough that it's a genuine generational leap, not just a speed bump. The BCM2712 SoC uses quad-core Cortex-A76 cores at 2.4GHz (versus the Pi 4's Cortex-A72 at 1.5GHz), giving roughly 2-3x the CPU throughput. The bigger structural change is invisible until you go looking for it: almost all I/O (USB, Ethernet, GPIO, camera/display) is no longer wired directly to the main SoC. It's handled by a new custom RP1 southbridge chip connected over an internal PCIe link — the same north-bridge/south-bridge split desktop PCs have used for decades. That split is also what unlocked the Pi line's first PCIe 2.0 x1 connector, exposed as a small FFC ribbon slot, for a genuine NVMe SSD.
simpleSummary: A faster, restructured successor to the Pi 4 with a real NVMe SSD option, an onboard clock battery, and a dedicated fan header.

specifications.processor: Broadcom BCM2712, quad-core Cortex-A76, 2.4 GHz (vs Cortex-A72 @ 1.5GHz on Pi 4)
specifications.gpu: VideoCore VII, supports OpenGL ES 3.1 and Vulkan 1.2
specifications.ram: 4GB / 8GB / 16GB LPDDR4X-4267 (the 2GB option from Pi 4 was dropped)
specifications.ioController: RP1 southbridge chip handles USB, Ethernet, GPIO, and camera/display I/O over an internal PCIe link — decoupled from the main SoC, unlike the Pi 4
specifications.storage: microSD (OS boot), plus PCIe 2.0 x1 NVMe SSD support via the FFC connector (requires a HAT+ or adapter board), USB boot supported
specifications.video: 2x micro-HDMI (dual 4K60 supported), 2x 4-lane MIPI camera/display connectors (combined CSI/DSI, replacing the Pi 4's separate single CSI + single DSI ports)
specifications.power: 5V/5A via USB-C with USB Power Delivery negotiation (27W max); an old 5V/3A Pi 4 supply still boots it but throttles peripherals
specifications.gpio: 40-pin header, 3.3V logic, physically and electrically pin-compatible with the Pi 4's layout
specifications.cooling: Runs noticeably hotter than the Pi 4 under sustained load; the official Active Cooler (fan + heatsink) is effectively required, not optional, for CPU-heavy workloads

pinMap.name: 3V3
pinMap.function: Regulated 3.3V output (two physical pins, same rail).

pinMap.name: 5V
pinMap.function: 5V rail, sourced from the USB-C input (two physical pins, same rail).
pinMap.currentLimit: Depends on power supply headroom; a weak supply here starves GPIO-powered peripherals before it starves the CPU.

pinMap.name: GND
pinMap.function: Common ground reference (multiple physical pins, all the same net).

pinMap.name: GPIO2 (SDA1)
pinMap.function: Default I2C data line, now routed through the RP1 chip rather than directly by the SoC.
pinMap.gotcha: Has a fixed onboard pull-up resistor, unlike most other GPIOs. Very tight bit-banged timing (unusual for I2C, but common on GPIO4/17 elsewhere) can behave slightly differently now that it's mediated by RP1 instead of the SoC directly.

pinMap.name: GPIO3 (SCL1)
pinMap.gotcha: Fixed onboard pull-up, same as GPIO2.

pinMap.name: GPIO14 (TXD)
pinMap.function: Hardware UART transmit, also used by the Linux serial console by default.
pinMap.gotcha: May be claimed by the OS console — disable serial console in raspi-config to reuse for a project.

pinMap.name: PCIE_FFC
pinMap.function: PCIe 2.0 x1 connector, exposed as a small flat-flex-cable (FFC) slot, for NVMe SSDs or other PCIe expansion boards via a HAT+ or adapter.
pinMap.gotcha: The FFC ribbon is fragile and easy to half-insert — a not-fully-seated cable causes the NVMe drive to be detected intermittently rather than cleanly fail. Booting from it also usually requires updating the bootloader EEPROM and setting PCIe boot order first.

pinMap.name: FAN_HEADER
pinMap.function: Dedicated 4-pin PWM-controlled fan connector for the official Active Cooler; new to the Pi 5, absent on Pi 4.
pinMap.gotcha: Only the official Active Cooler's connector matches this header's pinout/keying — generic fans wired here need checking against the pinout before assuming plug-and-play.

pinMap.name: RTC_BATTERY
pinMap.function: 2-pin connector for an optional CR2032-backed RTC battery, keeping the onboard real-time clock accurate across power loss.
pinMap.gotcha: No battery ships by default — without one, the RTC still exists in silicon but resets on every power loss, so the system clock is wrong at boot until it syncs over the network, same as a Pi 4.

pinMap.name: PWR_BUTTON
pinMap.function: Onboard power button header — first Pi with a real power button rather than just pulling the plug.
pinMap.gotcha: A single press is configurable behavior (shutdown, reboot, or nothing) — it does not always mean a safe shutdown happened unless configured that way, and a yanked power cord can still corrupt the SD card just like on a Pi 4.

pinMap.name: CAM_DSI
pinMap.function: Two identical 4-lane MIPI connectors that can each be configured as camera (CSI) or display (DSI) input — the Pi 4 had one fixed CSI port and one fixed DSI port instead.
pinMap.gotcha: Pi 4-era camera/display ribbon cables are a different connector pitch and are not physically compatible without an adapter cable, despite looking similar.

useCases.title: Faster on-device computer vision
useCases.scenario: Run larger or higher-resolution vision models (object detection, pose estimation) locally in near real time, something the Pi 4's CPU visibly struggled to keep up with.

useCases.title: NVMe-backed high-throughput data logger
useCases.scenario: Attach an NVMe SSD via the PCIe FFC connector for continuous high-speed sensor or video logging that would wear out a microSD card.

useCases.title: Offline field robot with correct timestamps
useCases.scenario: Add a CR2032 to the RTC battery header so a robot deployed without WiFi at boot still logs data with an accurate clock instead of defaulting to 1970.

useCases.title: Home automation hub with more headroom
useCases.scenario: Run Home Assistant plus more integrations and add-ons than a Pi 4 could handle smoothly, as the central server for a house of ESP32/ESP8266 sensor nodes.

useCases.title: Network-attached sensor logger
useCases.scenario: Read I2C sensors and log to a local database, served over the network via a small web dashboard.

useCases.title: Demanding retro emulation / media center
useCases.scenario: The extra CPU headroom makes more demanding emulators (PS2, GameCube-era) and higher-bitrate media playback practical compared to a Pi 4.

commonlyPairedWith: Arduino Uno (as a real-time I/O co-processor)
oftenConfusedWith: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (same GPIO pinout and form factor, but different SoC/I-O architecture and power requirements)
Raspberry Pi Pico (a microcontroller, not a computer, no OS)
oftenUpgradedTo: Jetson Orin Nano (when GPU-accelerated AI inference matters more than general CPU speed)

beginnerMistakes: Reusing a Raspberry Pi 4 power supply (5V/3A) — the Pi 5 wants 5V/5A over USB-C with PD negotiation, and an underpowered supply silently throttles USB and CPU performance instead of failing outright.

Skipping the Active Cooler or a heatsink — the Pi 5 draws meaningfully more power than a Pi 4 and throttles under sustained load without active cooling, unlike a Pi 4 that could often get away with passive-only in light use.
Assuming an NVMe drive on the PCIe FFC will boot immediately — it usually needs a bootloader EEPROM update and an explicit PCIe boot order change first.

Mis-seating the PCIe FFC ribbon cable — it's a fragile flex connector, and a half-inserted cable causes the drive to be intermittently undetected rather than cleanly fail, which reads like a software bug.

Assuming an old Pi 4 HAT that bit-bangs a timing-critical protocol behaves identically — GPIO is now routed through the RP1 chip instead of the SoC directly, and very tight timing-sensitive code can occasionally behave slightly differently.
